summary: KERNEL CONTEST: The Fair Use statutory exception (the codified legal kernel) read expansively as a structural right ensuring generative capacity and transformative use (a public scaffold) versus read strictly as a narrow, grudging defense to infringement (incumbent enclosure). The contest defines what constitutes permissible coordination versus actionable extraction[cite: 2, 3].

KERNEL CONTEST: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (the shared statutory kernel) read broadly via an 'incidental collection' framing that legitimizes domestic surveillance expansion versus a strict 'foreign-target-only' reading limiting executive reach. Each reading establishes different authority groundings and structural victim sets from the same text[cite: 2].

KERNEL CONTEST: The Constitution of the French Fifth Republic (the fixed text) read as a 'hyper-presidential' mandate granting near-unmediated sovereign power versus a parliamentary-constrained reading requiring legislative coordination. The document remains fixed, but the competing readings emit different constraints on democratic governance[cite: 2].

KERNEL CONTEST: The reciprocal oaths and codified obligations of medieval feudalism (the shared practice-norm kernel) read by the lord as a mandate for absolute economic extraction versus read by the vassal as a strictly bounded, conditional coordination mechanism. An inter-institutional contest over the exact limits of a shared commitment system[cite: 2, 3].
